items.title: Canadian negotiators dispel idea Canada can just play for time in trade talks with Trump
items.description: Canada’s top trade negotiators made the case behind closed doors Thursday for the government to seize the opportunity to strike a trade deal with The White House in the near term and not risk the economic pain of waiting out the final two years of the Trump administration.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s top trade negotiators made the case behind closed doors Thursday for the government to seize the opportunity to strike a trade deal with The White House in the near term and not risk the economic pain of waiting out the final two years of the Trump administration.
items.body:
OTTAWA – Canada’s top trade negotiators made the case behind closed doors Thursday for the government to seize the opportunity to strike a trade deal with The White House in the near term and not risk the economic pain of waiting out the final two years of the Trump administration.

That message was delivered to the federal government’s advisory committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, according to four sources familiar with the discussion.

While officials dispelled the notion that the best strategy was to wait out Donald Trump’s tenure, the sources also said there was no desire to accept a deal at any cost. Instead, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s closest advisers and officials made the case that tariff-affected businesses and sectors do not have an endless runway and for some, time is running short.

The message was delivered by Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette, Canadian Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman, and Privy Council Clerk Michael Sabia, the sources said.

It was the committee’s first meeting since the midterm elections that delivered a sharp rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The sources also said that while those election results have in some ways tilted the playing field in Canada’s favour, the vote was not significant enough to limit Trump’s tariff powers. The Canadian officials noted that even with a Democrat-controlled Congress, the U.S. president can still veto any bills sent to the White House and Canada does not believe there are enough votes in the Senate to overturn that veto with a supermajority.

Three of the sources also said that their takeaway from the discussion is that Canada is lukewarm on the prospect of striking an accord with Trump. Though the hope is to do so before Jan. 1 when the president has already threatened to further hike tariffs on vehicles, auto parts, and steel.

That message was echoed by committee member Erin O’Toole in an interview with Vassy Kapelos on CTV’s Power Play Thursday.

“We have to be realistic that the president will retain a veto,” O’Toole said. “So, even if a very positively inclined Congress starts removing presidential authority with respect to tariffs, the president could sort of dig in and fight this.”

“There’s still a ways to go,” he said. “The Americans know we’re not going to take any deal for the sake of the deal.”

The sources said work continues toward reaching an “interim deal” to address Section 232 tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum, and lumber as well as the Section 338 tariffs that are targeted at specific smaller industries and causing a lot of economic pain for small and medium sized businesses.

Trump and Carney have both publicly acknowledged progress in the talks, however, the officials told the meetings that sticking points remain in multiple areas, according to the sources. Two sources said the tariffs on autos are a key point of tension, but other sources said the negotiations are not yet resolved regarding many other sectors as well.

Three of the sources also said Charette warned the meeting attendees to be ready for more turbulence, and she explicitly noted the many powers that Trump still holds to ratchet up tariffs and broaden their application.

As CTV News previously reported, trade talks between Canada and the U.S. ramped up in October ahead of the U.S. midterms after falling apart in August.

The prime minister and U.S. president met on Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in Shenzen, China. Speaking virtually to the Dealbook summit from China later in the day, Carney reiterated Canada is willing to sign a deal that would benefit both countries but said “we’re not there yet.”

Auto tariffs were a key reason why talks to reach a deal in August failed. At the time, Carney said American negotiators were unwilling to lower the Section 232 tariffs on medium- and heavy-duty trucks. In sum, Carney told reporters in August that the proposals from the Americans on auto tariffs included “a series of terms that would have made the production more uneconomic over time.”

Two sources told CTV News on Thursday that neither the auto industry, nor the sectors affected by the Section 338 tariffs, can afford to wait two more years before meaningful tariff relief.

items.title: Liberals’ 2026 budget passes in House of Commons
items.description: Members of Parliament have voted to pass the 2026 federal budget in the House of Commons.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance and National Revenue Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne are seen on Parliament Hill before the federal budget in Ottawa, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Members of Parliament have voted to pass the 2026 federal budget in the House of Commons.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- Members of Parliament have voted to pass the 2026 federal budget in the House of Commons. 

Liberal MPs cheered and applauded as the Speaker announced the motion had passed with a vote of 162 to 151.

The budget, tabled Nov. 5, outlined billions of dollars in new borrowing and tax measures largely aimed at stimulating infrastructure construction and other capital projects.

Last year’s budget vote was a tense affair, as the minority Liberal government of the day needed members of other parties to either back its agenda or abstain from the vote to pass the spending plan.

Elizabeth May, then leader of the Green Party, cast the crucial vote that allowed Budget 2025 to pass, while two NDP and two Conservative MPs abstained or were absent.

Due to a series of byelections and floor-crossings over the last year, the Liberals now hold a majority of seats in the Commons, meaning the government can pass much of its agenda without the support of other parties.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has railed against the scale of the proposed borrowing in the budget, arguing it passes on costs to Canadians and fails to make life more affordable.

Parliamentary budget officer Annette Ryan published a series of reports this week scrutinizing Budget 2026. She also raised red flags about the total amount of borrowing on the horizon but found the government is narrowly on track to maintain its fiscal anchors.

Improved revenues from better-than-expected economic results and a tailwind of tax dollars from higher global oil prices have improved the government’s bottom line since the spring.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says the budget meets an uncertain moment by leveraging Canada’s relatively strong fiscal position to invest in its future.

Liberal members of Parliament clapped when Champagne voted in favour of the budget on Thursday, with the minister raising his arms in triumph. 

“Confident countries invest,” Champagne told a Senate committee on Tuesday when asked why the government opted to spend much of its recent fiscal windfall rather than meaningfully paying down the deficit.

“We’re one of the very few countries in the G7 who can afford to do that, which is investing in the growth, but at the same time supporting Canadians at the time of need … with affordability measures,” he said.

Proposals in Budget 2026 such as the $36-billion productivity mega-deduction are aimed at convincing businesses to invest more in their own machinery and boost worker productivity.

Other budget measures would top up the Groceries and Essentials Benefit for lower-income families, offer support to Canada’s cultural sectors and ramp up efforts to eliminate homelessness.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis told reporters Thursday his party’s MPs would vote against the budget, which he argues caters to the needs of big business.

“Canadians need a budget that delivers real solutions to lower the cost of living: groceries, cellphones, housing and health care,” he said.

The budget’s title — “Maîtres Chez Nous,” or “Masters of our Destiny — borrows a phrase from Quebec’s Quiet Revolution, a period of rapid socio-economic change in the province.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet has criticized the Liberals’ use of the phrase, arguing the budget doesn’t give the province more control over its own affairs.

Even after a budget passes a vote, there are more hurdles to clear before its various proposals are enacted.

The government will go on to table one or more budget implementation bills. Those bills go through committee studies and votes and might be amended before passing into law.

The Liberals’ second budget implementation act for the 2025 budget wasn’t tabled until May of this year and is still working its way through Parliament. It includes provisions to deliver automatic federal benefits to low-income households and implement a framework for reporting cryptocurrency assets.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.description: KPMG Canada says some client files were compromised after a cybersecurity breach that involved unauthorized access by a third party to certain tax documents.

items._ogDesc: KPMG Canada says some client files were compromised after a cybersecurity breach that involved unauthorized access by a third party to certain tax documents.
items.body:
OTTAWA - KPMG Canada says some client files were compromised after a cybersecurity breach that involved unauthorized access by a third party to certain tax documents.

The accounting firm would not say when the breach occurred, how many clients were affected or the number of files accessed.

The company said it acted immediately to secure its systems and is reaching out to those impacted.

“We are confident we have protected our clients’ information and, based on our ongoing monitoring, the information impacted by this incident is not available online or being misused for any purpose,” spokesperson Sonja Cloutier-Bosworth wrote in a statement.

Tech analyst Carmi Levy says that may not be the case.

“The cybercriminals get to determine where the data goes, who accesses it, who pays for it and what’s done with it,” Levy said. “So they’re saying it because it feels like the right thing to say, but it shouldn’t make anyone feel safer. The data’s been exposed, it’s too late.”

This breach comes after an alert in October from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security warned about an ongoing voice phishing or “vishing” scam targeting organizations in the legal and financial sectors.

The alert stated that “multiple Canadian firms have been targeted by individuals impersonating internal IT support and directing employees to fraudulent sign-in pages” and typically involved someone using Microsoft Teams or phone calls.

“Any cyberattack against any victim, of course, is problematic. It is especially galling when the victim is a high-profile law firm or a tax firm or professional services firm, where they have the resources to fund large IT departments, cybersecurity teams,” Levy said.

He said there are ways for people to protect themselves, including using a strong password, limiting what’s shared on social media and using features like two-factor authentication and encryption.

Levy said the risks are going to get worse as artificial intelligence becomes more pervasive.

“It makes it a lot easier for them to cover more ground to target us with even more sophisticated and powerful attacks,” he said.

The Credit Counselling Society (CCS) suggests anyone impacted should determine what information was exposed and, if sensitive information was involved, consider adding a fraud alert to their credit file.

“It’s not just the fact that documents were accessed. It’s about how that information can be used, right?” said Ali Harris-Saunders with the society. “We’re not at a stage of panic by any means, but it is important to act quickly, remain diligent, and monitor your bank accounts and your credit accounts.”

items.title: Elon Musk’s Tesla is the biggest beneficiary of Canada’s China EV policy so far
items.description: It appears the biggest beneficiary so far of reducing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles is the company founded by Elon Musk, a staunch ally of U.S. President Donald Trump.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Left: Tesla CEO Elon Musk (The Associated Press). Right: The Peace Tower on Parliament Hill (The Canadian Press).]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: It appears the biggest beneficiary so far of reducing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles is the company founded by Elon Musk, a staunch ally of U.S. President Donald Trump.
items.body:
OTTAWA - If trade talks with the Americans fails to protect Canadian auto jobs, Prime Minister Mark Carney has said he would consider turning to Chinese automakers.

But amid the tough talk and contingency planning, it appears the biggest beneficiary so far of reducing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles is the company spearheaded by Elon Musk, a staunch ally of U.S. President Donald Trump.

As part of a strategic partnership signed with the People’s Republic of China in January, Canada agreed to allow the importation of 49,000 EVs from China this fiscal year. Tariffs on the vehicles were reduced from 100 per cent to the “most-favored-nation” tariff rate of 6.1 per cent.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The quota applies to vehicles manufactured in China, but not specifically Chinese companies.

Since March, Canada has imported 16,211 EVs that were built in China. This is approximately 32,000 vehicles shy of the 49,000 EV quota for this year that Carney had negotiated with Xi.

Tesla has a factory in Shanghai, which is its main export hub for Canada, Europe and the Asia-Pacific region.

In October, Tesla announced on its website that it was pausing orders for its Shanghai-built Model 3 Premium cars because of “high demand” that exhausted its import quota. A banner on its site, states that: “Ordering resumes if Govt of Canada issues more quota, expected March 2027.”

Adam Chambers, the Conservative shadow minister for innovation, science and industry said that he was told “90 per cent of the quotas have gone to Tesla.”

“Would Canadians be happy to know so far that Tesla so far is the primary beneficiary of the Chinese electric vehicle policy? Is that the intention for that to continue for the government? Is the intention to enrich Mr. Musk?”

Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla has raised the ire of Canadians through his posts on X.

Musk has often used the social media platform he owns to weigh in on Canadian politics. He’s posted that Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate from the country and has posted that Canada “is not a real country.”

When asked about Chambers’ “90 per cent” figure, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said he didn’t have the “recent numbers,” but acknowledged that “Tesla obviously manufactures in China and some of that quota in the past has been used for Tesla vehicles.”

More Chinese EV companies to get certification

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu has acknowledged that the majority of Chinese-made EVs that have entered the Canadian market “are Teslas around $40,000.”

While in Manila, Philippines for the ASEAN summit, Sidhu said that more Chinese EV brands are expected next year after the companies go through the Transport Canada certification process.

Sidhu said that the companies are preparing by investing in charging infrastructure and building up dealerships.

“Every time I sit down with them it’s about Canadian supply chains. It’s about utilizing Canadian workers,” Sidhu told reporters last Saturday.

In an update, Global Affairs Canada said that a “second original equipment manufacturer that is based in China has fulfilled all Transport Canada requirements and has just started importing vehicles into Canada.” The backgrounder stated the newly arrived EVs are expected to have an import price of less than $35,000.

The government is not releasing the name of the companies that have cleared the regulatory hurdles.

In June, BYD announced on social media that it planned to launch in Canada by the end of 2026 and that it would open 20 branded dealerships in Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal and Calgary.

Other Chinese companies that have expressed interest in selling EVs in Canada include Dongfeng, Geely and Chery.

Jody Thomas, Canada’s former national security advisor, who worked for former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, says there are real security concerns with Chinese EVs.

“I would not buy a Chinese EV,” Thomas told CTV’s Power Play. “Anybody who buys a Chinese EV needs to understand that all the information about what they do, where they go, will get sent back to the Chinese government.”

The Carney government says that the Chinese EV quota will represent three per cent of the total auto market in Canada. But as the number of vehicles grows, Transport Minister Mackinnon says, the government will conduct a review to analyze limiting where Chinese EV’s can drive.

items.title: Trump administration auctions deep-sea mining leases near American Samoa in first sale of its kind
items.description: The Trump administration auctioned deep-sea mining leases to millions of acres of the federal seafloor, giving a controversial industry a foothold in U.S. waters.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka plays with her daughter Erhys at Fatumafuti Beach near Pago Pago, American Samoa, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (AP Photo/Annika Hammerschlag)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Annika Hammerschlag</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Trump administration auctioned deep-sea mining leases to millions of acres of the federal seafloor, giving a controversial industry a foothold in U.S. waters.
items.body:
The Trump administration on Thursday auctioned deep-sea mining leases to millions of acres of the federal seafloor near American Samoa, giving a controversial industry a foothold in U.S. waters.

The two 20-year leases are the first of their kind in the U.S., following U.S. President Donald Trump’s directive last year to leverage deep-ocean minerals to counter growing competition for resources from China. The leases are already the source of several legal challenges.

The two lease areas each sold for the minimum bid amount of US$3 million to deep-sea mining startup Wetstone U.S. Ventures, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. While there were two bidders at the auction, only Wetstone placed bids. Wetstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press.

  • Latest updates on international news here

The leases grant the company the ability to begin initial surveys of the seafloor to explore for minerals and prepare their testing or mining plans. It has the exclusive right to mine those areas commercially if approved in further environmental reviews.

The auction moved forward despite passionate opposition from locals in the territory and three lawsuits seeking to halt the sales. The auction was held at the Ventura County Fire Department Headquarters in Southern California, where a few dozen protesters gathered outside.

“We had hoped it would never come to this,” Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, an American Samoa resident who has fought the auction for more than a year, said in a statement Thursday.

Globally, deep-sea mining is still at an experimental stage. A handful of other countries have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals, but no company has started commercial operations. The U.S. has never issued a lease for deep-sea minerals beyond a short-lived mining effort in California waters more than 60 years ago.

The federal interest in seafloor minerals stems from an April 2025 executive order, when the president directed his administration to search for and responsibly develop critical minerals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. The Marine Minerals Administration is considering further auctions of the seabed near the Northern Mariana Islands, Virginia and Alaska, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters.

It’s unclear if the leases will withstand legal challenge. On Monday, a court ordered the National Marine Fisheries Service to more thoroughly assess the impacts the mining activities could have on endangered species, saying the agency’s “cramped, expedited, informal” review violated the Endangered Species Act.

  • Latest updates on commodities here

The Marine Minerals Administration said in a statement that it had addressed the court’s opinion by starting to consult with the fisheries service on another environmental assessment. But it did not cancel or delay the auction.

David Henkin, deputy managing attorney at the environmental law group Earthjustice, said the ruling made Thursday’s auction unlawful. In order to issue the notice of sale, the government needed to comply with the Endangered Species Act, he said.

“We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton said in a statement. Earthjustice is representing Fa’asao Amerika Samoa, a group dedicated to safeguarding the territory’s culture, and the Conservation Council of Hawaii in the suit.

Another lawsuit filed Wednesday by the Natural Resources Defense Council and Finafinau, an environmental group founded by Suluai-Mahuka, similarly argues the environmental review process was rushed and is asking the court to strike down the leases.

A third lawsuit, brought by a council of local chiefs in American Samoa, the Faleula o le Manu’atele, is challenging the federal government’s authority to auction the waters near their islands.

Tony Romeo, head of the deep-sea mining startup Eco Minerals, which did not participate in the auction, said any company going into deep-sea mining needs to be prepared for pushback from environmental groups.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

“If they can halt it through legal action, they will,” he said. “We’ll see how it ultimately plays out.”

Erik Milito, president of the National Ocean Industries Association, said in a statement that he expects industry interest and investment to grow in the coming years.

“Decades of environmental research and extensive assessments have helped lay the groundwork for responsible ocean mineral development,” he said.

Helen Wieffering, The Associated Press

items.title: Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers
items.description: Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Digital billboards advertise Anthropic on the day of its IPO in Times Square, New York, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Seth Wenig</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company.
items.body:
Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking all records for money raised on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company.

The price tag on its shares was enough to put the value of the San Francisco company well beyond US$1 trillion.

That kind of number was once unheard of for a company’s first moments trading on the stock market. But an acceleration in corporate wealth — and most recently the AI boom — has changed that. Anthropic is the second business to debut with a value over a trillion dollars (following SpaceX just months ago), and will join a handful of other tech giants that measure their wealth by figures reaching 13 digits.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Time will tell how Anthropic ultimately fares on the public market. The Claude maker decided to proceed with its IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, fears of a possible AI bubble and growing unease among the public about the technology’s risks overall.

Here are some numbers to help understand Thursday’s IPO.

The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: US$81 billion

That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of trading on Thursday, it offered 980 million shares priced at US$83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about US$75 billion in June.

The next biggest IPO hauls went to South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix (US$26.5 billion in July) and oil giant Saudi Aramco (US$25.6 billion in 2019).

Anthropic’s initial valuation: US$1.5 trillion

The initial price per share was set at US$83. But in early trading, that spiked more than 30 per cent — to US$111.50 a share — pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to US$2.01 trillion just before noon ET.

By market close Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at US$97.17 per share. That’s still over 17 per cent higher than its initial public offering price.

In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of US$2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion.

Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S&P 500: 11

Apple currently leads the pack at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S&P 500 index yet.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over US$1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018.

How far a trillion U.S. dollar bills would stretch if laid end to end: 93 million miles

That would surpass the roughly 93 million miles (150 million kilometres) between Earth and the sun.

The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. US$1 trillion is a thousand times greater than US$1 billion. And a million times more than US$1 million.

There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the U.S. Census Bureau. If US$1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost US$122.

Wyatte Grantham-Philips, The Associated Press

items.title: Anthropic closes first day of trading at US$97.17, jumping more than 17% above its initial public offering price
items.description: The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened for trading Thursday in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Anthropic logo is displayed on the Nasdaq MarketSite tower as part of the Anthropic IPO in New York, Thursday, Nov.19, 2026. (AP Photo/Andres Kudacki)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Andres Kudacki</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened for trading Thursday in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble.
items.body:
NEW YORK — The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened for trading Thursday in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety that the technology threatens lives and livelihoods.

Anthropic shares began trading at US$111.50, spiking more than 30 per cent above the initial public offering price, before closing at US$97.17, more than 17 per cent higher than the IPO.

A day earlier, the company priced its IPO at US$83 per share, enough to value the entire business at US$1.5 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record. At the start of trading, the valuation leaped to US$2.01 trillion.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The initial price was surprisingly high given that investor worries had ratcheted up even more recently following the stunning ouster of AI’s chief promoter, the CEO of Nvidia, in a possible Chinese spying scandal. Anthropic had earlier set a much lower price range between US$70 to US$78 per share.

“It’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia,” said Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co. “The pricing shows strong demand among investors.”

A big test remains if investors maintain the classic “IPO pop” by keeping the stock aloft in its first day — or if it will tumble by the close.

The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool offered 980 million shares to the public, which at US$83 per share translated into proceeds of US$81 billion.

Anthropic’s soaring debut on Wall Street was not enough to carry the rest of the market. U.S. stock indexes fell after a morning rally quickly evaporated.

IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt

In addition to market jitters over AI, the IPO is facing down a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. For its part, Anthropic rival OpenAI decided to postpone its initial offering until next year.

The company, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, is also facing big financial challenges ahead.

Anthropic already has taken on US$6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

While the company showed ample cash in its last financial report, it would have likely run through it quickly given its outsize spending plans. In the same financial report, the company said it had signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend US$900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including US$70 billion in the next 12 months.

Such massive spending by AI companies, comparable to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads, have scared lenders, helping to push borrowing rates high recently.

With the IPO, though, Anthropic will now have enormous resources to accelerate its expansion without taking on more debt. The offering will also allow its employees to sell vested stock, making many of them millionaires overnight — and potentially adding billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei.

AI industry faces concerns about data centres, a possible bubble and regulations

Founded five years ago by the siblings along with several other former OpenAI veterans, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.

Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.

Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.

In comments at the opening bell Thursday, Amodei sought to dampen fears by stressing a commitment to ensure humans are in control of the technology.

“If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same,” he said. ”The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.”

Amid mounting fears, the regulatory environment could change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry as a backlash unfolds against data centres. And two big states offering incentives for data centres, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors who have vowed to stop new construction.

In his comments Thursday, Amodei also touted a range of positive uses for AI, noting that Claude already is helping scientists do quicker research and that the technology could help accelerate that progress in the future.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

“Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox and polio history for most of the world,” he said, “but progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families.”

He also pointed to Claude’s use across companies, nonprofits and government services. “I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future,” he said.

Adding to the pressure to go public was the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.

Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.

“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said Tuesday in an interview with The Associated Press at the Semafor Silicon Valley & the World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”

Bernard Condon and Barbara Ortutay, The Associated Press

Ortutay reported from Oakland, California. Associated Press business writers Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Michelle Chapman in New York contributed.

items._ogDesc: The U.S. stock market is tumbling again Thursday as beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence keep falling on worries their breathtaking boom may be over.
items.body:
NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market tumbled again as beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence kept falling Thursday on worries their breathtaking boom may be over. The losses came even though a leading AI lab, Anthropic, found a strong welcome for the debut of its own stock on Wall Street.

The S&P 500 dropped two per cent for a sixth straight loss. That’s its longest losing streak in two and a half years, and the index at the heart of many 401(k) accounts is now down 8.2 per cent from its all-time high set last month.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101 points, or 2.2 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3 per cent.

  • Dow Jones updates here

The losses were widespread, and more than 90 per cent of the stocks that make up the S&P 500 index fell.

Leading them downward was Williams-Sonoma, which dropped 15.2 per cent after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was a bit weaker than Wall Street expected. It also stuck with its forecast for how much revenue it will make throughout 2026, and the midpoint of that range was below what analysts were expecting.

Walmart sank one per cent even though it reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations.

For a while Thursday morning, gains for several AI-related stocks seemed to be enough to more than make up for such losses.

The S&P 500 jumped as much as 1.3 per cent after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold shares of its stock at US$83 apiece in its initial public offering. That’s more than the US$70 to US$78 it earlier thought it would get, and its price quickly surged above US$115 after it began trading on the Nasdaq shortly before noon.

Anthropic later pared its gain and finished the day at US$97.17, still up 17.1 per cent.

Even before its stock began trading, the strong demand for Anthropic’s IPO appeared to demonstrate faith remained among investors in the AI revolution. The industry needed a boost following sharp recent drops for AI-related stocks on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

But AI stocks quickly returned to their jittery ways in what Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, called “a very turbulent, white-knuckle period.”

Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared because of the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8 per cent and then swung to a loss of 2.1 per cent.

CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, went from a 10.5 per cent leap in the morning to a drop of 6.1 per cent.

Nvidia erased its early gain of 4.7 per cent and flipped to a loss of 3.3 per cent amid the lengthening list of worries dogging the entire industry.

At first it was criticism that AI stocks had broadly gone into a bubble after shooting so high, along with doubts that AI could produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments in data centres worth it. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund the industry’s growth. Then came this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections, which raised concerns about more regulation for AI.

Most recently, it was the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. He was one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth.

Other companies, meanwhile, offered more encouraging signals about AI.

Palo Alto Networks climbed 6.4 per cent after the AI cybersecurity company topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also agreed to buy Applied Compute, a platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models, to help customers adopt AI securely. The all-stock deal is valued at US$4.5 billion.

Everpure, a company that helps businesses manage and store their data, said its revenue jumped last quarter by more than analysts expected in part because of AI-related offerings. Everpure’s stock rose 4.7 per cent.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 147.80 points to 7,175.83. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101.11 to 49,097.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 550.69 to 23,879.20.

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased as the drops for stock prices sent investors toward investments seen as safer. When prices for Treasury bonds go up, their yields go down, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.04 per cent from 5.07 per cent Wednesday.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Also weighing on yields were a couple reports on the U.S. economy that came in weaker than economists expected. One said slightly more U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, though the number remains low compared with history. Another said manufacturing growth in the mid-Atlantic region is slowing by more than economists expected.

In stock markets abroad, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7 per cent. Helping to lead the way was SoftBank Group, which climbed 4.6 per cent. It was an early investor in OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and competitor to Anthropic.

South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent thanks to strength for its stocks tied to the AI boom, but stocks were weaker elsewhere in Asia and in Europe. Germany’s DAX lost 1.1 per cent.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writer Chan Ho-him contributed.

items._ogDesc: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc gave an update on trade talks Thursday at a meeting of an advisory committee on economic relations with the U.S. — the first such meeting since midterm elections delivered a sharp rebuke of the Trump administration.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc gave an update on trade talks Thursday at a meeting of an advisory committee on economic relations with the U.S. — the first such meeting since midterm elections delivered a sharp rebuke of the Trump administration.

The Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations discussed on Thursday “the evolving Canada-U.S. trade relationship and Canada’s approach to advancing its economic interests,” according to a readout from Global Affairs Canada.

The virtual meeting also included Canadian Ambassador to the United States Mark Wiseman and Canada’s chief trade negotiator Janice Charette.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada rapidly escalated after negotiations broke down in August. Ottawa and Washington each accused the other of putting eleventh-hour demands on the table.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said at the time that Trump’s team wanted to restrict Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries, endanger Canada’s protections for language and culture, and maintain hefty tariffs on some automobiles.

In response, Trump hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs and banned imports of others. He threatened to further increase duties in January if no deal is made by then.

The president also signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The Trump administration’s tone on Canada softened somewhat after midterm election exit polling indicated that the president’s trade war and his sweeping tariff agenda were unpopular with American voters.

Carney and Trump met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific economic summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. Following the meeting, the prime minister said a “very good trade arrangement” with the United States is possible but Canada won’t just sit around and wait.

During a meeting Tuesday of the House of Commons international trade committee in Ottawa, LeBlanc and Charette told MPs a deal was still possible.

They also cautioned there is no guarantee Canada can restore the terms of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, better known as CUSMA.

Charette said Canada has to prepare for a world where a tariff-free arrangement may no longer be possible.

The objective is to “get to the lowest rate of tariff on the narrowest basket of goods with the most preferential access for Canadian businesses and Canadian workers,” Charette said.

The committee, which includes representatives of the business community, trade organizations and organized labour, was created by Carney last April.

It has held 10 meetings to strategize responses to Trump’s unpredictable tariffs and discuss CUSMA’s future.

The Trump administration chose not to renew CUSMA in July. The decision triggered a rolling annual review for up to a decade, at which point the agreement will expire if the three countries cannot agree on an extension.

“Committee members brought forward insights from their respective sectors and regions, highlighting the challenges businesses and workers continue to face because of U.S. trade measures,” Thursday’s readout said.

“The discussion also addressed the implementation of federal measures to support Canadian businesses and workers affected by U.S. tariffs, including the effectiveness of existing supports and opportunities to better respond to the needs of affected businesses.”

By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

items.description: The approved project comprises a 24-storey concrete tower and 2-storey townhouse and an amenity building
items._ogDesc: The approved project comprises a 24-storey concrete tower and 2-storey townhouse and an amenity building
items.body:
A partially-built residential high-rise building in Surrey’s City Centre, that is under a court-ordered sale, is back on the market.

Appearing to have found a buyer as it was listed this summer as being under contract, the project in the 13000-block of 101 Avenue is once again available, listed at $30 million.

“Construction on the project has progressed to the sixth floor above grade. Buyers can restart construction and benefit from over $23 million in hard costs spent to date, along with fully paid for entitlements and completed design drawings,” the listing notes.

It had been marketed as “Centra,”an approved project comprising a 24-storey concrete tower and a two-storey townhouse and amenity building.

The project has 167 residential units above 194 stalls in two levels of underground parking.

The listing also notes, “Prior to construction delays, the project was successfully pre-sold; however, all contracts have since been rescinded, offering a new owner a clean slate to relaunch a sales program or reposition the asset as a market rental.”

Construction on the project ceased in August 2024 and Alvarez & Marsal Canada Inc. was appointed the receiver and manager earlier this year.

Home sales forecast to move up in Greater Vancouver next year

A new report by the British Columbia Real Estate Association (BCREA) forecasts home sales in Greater Vancouver going up, however, prices won’t correspond to that level of increase.

The BCREA’s 2026 Fourth Quarter Housing Forecast notes Multiple Listing Service (MLS) residential sales in BC are forecast to fall 4.5 per cent to 67,025 units this year.

The report notes that with active listings near their highest level since 2015, and additional pressure from elevated new-home inventory, the BCREA anticipates the average price in B.C. will fall by 1.2 per cent in 2026.

That decrease largely reflects disproportionate weakness in more expensive markets in the Lower Mainland, casting downward pressure on the broader provincial average price, the report explains.

In 2027, MLS residential sales are forecast to move higher, rising 7.2 per cent to 71,840 units.

Greater Vancouver is forecast to see an 8.7 per cent increase in 2027, after seeing decreases the previous two years.

The Fraser Valley is forecast to see an increase of 9.1 per cent.

The 2027 average MLS price is forecast to go up 2.2 per cent in Greater Vancouver and 1.8 per cent in the Fraser Valley.

“British Columbia’s housing market continues to face a challenging economic environment, as mounting headwinds fuel hesitancy among prospective buyers,” said BCREA Chief Economist Brendon Ogmundson in a news release. “Ultimately, we expect a modest recovery in home sales in 2027 as the impacts of new United States tariffs fade and fixed mortgage rates decline.”

items.title: Tracking Toronto’s 5 Tallest Rental, Condo Proposals (So Far) This Fall
items.description:
Toronto has never been shy about building up, and newsy developments like the Pinnacle towers and One Bloor West are proof that the high-rise fixation is alive and well.

But it’s not just the 80-storey-plus cohort that’s worth paying attention to. If you sift through the steady stream of development applications hitting the City’s desk, proposals in the the 40- to 60-storey range are impressive in their own rights, promising to add hundreds of new homes to the city while reshaping neighbourhood skylines.

Since September, there have been a handful of proposals that fit that bill, including a 56-storey rental that would displace the century-old City Morgue, a pair of 46-storey condos that have come out the other side of receivership, and a 61-storey condo slated for the burgeoning Etobicoke City Centre area. Here’s what's planned.

56 Storeys: 86 and 100-108 Lombard St and 103 Richmond St E

Rendering of 86 and 100-108 Lombard St and 103 Richmond St E/WZMH Architects

After initially proposing a 59-storey mixed-use building in 2022, Forum Asset Management and Slate Asset Management secured OLT approvals in 2025 for a much taller, 72-storey tower at 86 and 100-108 Lombard Street and 103 Richmond Street East — a parcel in Toronto’s Old Town area.

The most recent version of the proposal is considerably scaled back, describing a 56-storey mixed-use building (exclusive of a two-storey mechanical penthouse). The other major way the development departs from past plans is the unit tenure; while the 2022 proposal asked for 480 condo units, and the 2025 settlement was for 702 condo units, Forum and Slate are now planning 523 purpose-built rental units, alongside space for office and retail. The heritage-designated former City Morgue building at 86 Lombard Street would be relocated to the eastern portion of the development site to make way for the proposed.

Learn more.

50 Storeys & 50 Storeys: 60 Overlea Blvd

Rendering of 60 Overlea Blvd/Sweeny&Co Architects

The Ontario Line is inching towards the finish line, and 60 Overlea Boulevard in Thorncliffe Park — currently occupied by an under-utilized retail plaza — is one of the many Toronto addresses that will benefit from the forthcoming transit connectivity. The site is less than 500 metres from the future Thorncliffe Park station, and a proposal from landowner Plazaworks Inc. describes a pair of 50-storey towers with a shared podium. All 1,261 units would be rental in tenure, while the ground floor would be reserved for non-residential uses, including a potential childcare facility.

Plazaworks is also seeking official plan and zoning bylaw amendments to re-designate the property from General Employment Areas to Mixed Use Areas, which would pave the way for some of the proposed non-residential space to be used for “employment-generating uses.”

Learn more.

46 Storeys & 46 Storeys: 7 Labatt Ave And 77 River St

Rendering of 7 Labatt Ave and 77 River St/Giannone Petricone Associates

A long-stalled development site at 7 Labatt Avenue and 77 River Street — on the edge of Regent Park, about a kilometre from the future Corktown station of the Ontario Line — is now under the ownership of KingSett Capital, with the firm now planning a pair of 46-storey towers. The high-rises would have 1,170 condo units between them, while a separate two-storey Salvation Army building is planned to the east (replacing the Salvation Army building currently at 7 Labatt). The plans also include a publicly accessible open space running between the 46-storey towers.

The site was initially being redeveloped by TAS in favour of their “Labatt Village” project, set to include 48- and 44-storey buildings with 1,240 units. The project was placed under receivership in February, and KingSett took over through an $84.15-million credit bid this summer, paving the way for the site’s next chapter.

Learn more.

50 Storeys: 4632-4648 Yonge St and 16-18 Cameron Ave

Rendering of 4632-4648 Yonge St and 16-18 Cameron Ave/Arcadis

While some developments hinge on the forthcoming Ontario Line, others make use of the transit Toronto already has. A proposal from Yonge and Cameron LP is for a 50-storey mixed-use tower at 4632–4648 Yonge Street and 16–18 Cameron Avenue in North York, where it would replace a two-storey commercial plaza and two detached houses around 200 metres from the Sheppard-Yonge subway station. The site is also within the North York Centre and a designated Protected Major Transit Station Area, where the City is encouraging further intensification.

The development would introduce 569 new residential units to the site — all condo in tenure — and the continued operation of the existing autobody shop at 4656 Yonge. The tower would also include ground-floor retail and indoor and outdoor amenity spaces designed with families with children and pet owners in mind.

Learn more.

61 Storeys: 1234 Islington Ave

Rendering of 1234 Islington Ave/Sweeny&Co Architects

After securing City Council approvals in June, Montez Corporation has moved ahead with site plan control application for a 61-storey mixed-use tower at 1243 Islington Avenue in central Etobicoke, where it would replace a 12-storey office building. Though the City approved 702 condo units and a retail component for the site, the latest planning documents show that the unit-count has been cut down to 527. In addition, it seems the project has been switched to purpose-built rental, and 16 units are planned to be affordable.

The site is less than 200 metres from Islington Station, within a Protected Major Transit Station Area, and leans into a wider push to reshape the neighbourhood into a more complete community. Nearby, the new Etobicoke Civic Centre is coming up on what’s locally known as the Westwood Theatre Lands, where it will accommodate a new library, recreation centre, child-care centre, public health clinic, and civic square.

items.title: OSFI cuts capital rules for small banks to boost mortgage competition
items.description: Smaller lenders gain room to compete for mortgage clients under OSFI’s latest capital changes
items.content: <p>Smaller lenders gain room to compete for mortgage clients under OSFI’s latest capital changes</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307089600249717.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Smaller lenders gain room to compete for mortgage clients under OSFI’s latest capital changes
items.body:
Canada’s banking regulator moved to ease capital constraints on the country’s smaller lenders, launching a Competitive Prudential Initiative designed to narrow the structural gap between smaller institutions and the dominant Big Six in key lending markets, including residential mortgages.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) announced the initiative as the centrepiece of its fourth Quarterly Release of 2026.

The changes target small and medium-sized banks (SMSBs) and federal credit unions, reducing risk-weighted assets — the measure determining how much capital a lender must hold against potential loan losses — across residential mortgages, small and medium-sized business lending, and corporate lending.

Under the proposals, the risk weight for loans to small and medium-sized businesses would fall to 65% from 75%, while corporate lending risk weights would drop to 80% from 100%.

OSFI will also reduce capital requirements for residential mortgages with credit bureau scores above 720.

Levelling the playing field

The move addresses a structural imbalance that has long given Canada’s domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs) a capital advantage over their smaller rivals.

Peter Routledge, Superintendent of Financial Institutions at OSFI, called it “our most ambitious effort to date to level the playing field in Canadian banking without materially impacting the resilience of the system,” adding that the initiative was about “giving smaller deposit-takers greater room for prudent risk-taking.”

The changes align with Budget 2026, which proposes amending the OSFI Act to introduce a secondary competition mandate, formally requiring the regulator to weigh competitive balance alongside financial stability.

Ottawa has proposed Bank Act amendments to widen banking competition, with broader measures directly targeting the Big Six’s hold on the sector.

What it means for brokers

For mortgage brokers, a wider field of better-capitalised smaller lenders could translate into greater product diversity and more competitive rate options for clients.

Brokers command a 33% share of the Canadian mortgage market, up four percentage points since 2022, according to Mortgage Professionals Canada’s 2024 Mid-Year Report.

Naga Parvatharajan, chief executive of Ratehub.ca in Canada, has described the broader direction of competition reform as “exactly the kind of structural signal that tells fintech innovators, consumers and incumbents: this market is open for business.”

He added that “when more institutions enter the market, Canadians gain better rates and innovative options,” and stressed the need for follow-through: “This is a meaningful step forward, but now we must ensure the entire ecosystem evolves in tandem.”

The initiative builds on OSFI’s June decision to lower the Domestic Stability Buffer, releasing an estimated $74 billion in excess capital from Canada’s six largest banks.

Proposed changes are open for public consultation until February 17, 2027, with final guidelines expected in late 2027 or early 2028.

items.description: Ontario court certifies Scotiabank class action over unpaid vacation and holiday pay claims
items.content: <p>Ontario court certifies Scotiabank class action over unpaid vacation and holiday pay claims</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307048260813539.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Ontario court certifies Scotiabank class action over unpaid vacation and holiday pay claims
items.body:
An Ontario court has certified a class action lawsuit against The Bank of Nova Scotia (Scotiabank) alleging the lender failed to pay vacation pay and statutory holiday pay owed to thousands of current and former home financing advisers (HFAs) under the Canada Labour Code (CLC).

The Ontario Superior Court of Justice certified the case — Deacon v. Bank of Nova Scotia, 2026 ONSC 1793 — on March 31.

The representative plaintiffs are Nathalie Deacon, a current Scotiabank HFA, and Gail Ouellette, a retired HFA, both represented by Paliare Roland Rosenberg Rothstein LLP, a Toronto-based litigation firm.

Scotiabank denies all allegations, and no claims have been proven in court.

What the class action alleges

The suit contends that Scotiabank, one of Canada’s Big Six banks with approximately $1.5 trillion in assets as at April 30, excluded variable pay components when calculating vacation and statutory holiday pay entitlements for its HFAs — a commission-based role within its real estate secured lending division.

For retired class members, the plaintiffs further allege the bank failed to calculate pension entitlements based on total compensation.

The class covers all HFAs, including those previously carrying the title of Mortgage Development Manager, employed between November 1, 2009, and March 31, 2026.

The Ontario Class Proceedings Fund provided financial backing for the case and would receive 10% of any recovery if the action succeeds.

The timing places the certification within a period of considerable internal change at Scotiabank. The bank eliminated approximately 3,000 roles through its late-2025 restructuring, drawing sustained scrutiny to its employment practices.

That same period also saw new senior appointments to its real estate secured lending and risk units in November 2025, as the bank pushed to accelerate its broader transformation strategy.

Scotiabank reported net income of $2.95 billion for the three months ended July 31, the strongest quarter in its history.

The certification adds to pressure on federally regulated lenders over how commission-based staff compensation is structured. 

Compensation is one of the three factors mortgage professionals consistently rank highest when choosing where to work.

“The strongest organizations invest in their people through mentorship, coaching, and real career development rather than simply focusing on production. They understand that mortgage professionals are running businesses within a business,” Michelle Campbell, mortgage broker at MA – A Better Way Mortgage Group, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in March.

“Professionals also want growth opportunities, which could be mentorship roles, leadership pathways, specialization in certain lending areas, or business coaching.”

items.title: Toronto commercial real estate investment already outpaces 2025
items.description: Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore
items.content: <p>Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307039780020741.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore
items.body:
Toronto commercial real estate investment has already surpassed its full-year 2025 total. Nearly $13.5 billion in transactions closed across the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) in the first nine months of 2026, according to Avison Young’s Greater Toronto investment review for the third quarter. That total is up 55% from the same period last year.

Third-quarter volume reached $4.4 billion, a 52% gain from Q3 2025, though 22% below a stronger second quarter. The number of trades rose a more modest 16% year to date, to 1,356.

“The much larger rise in dollar volume versus number of transactions is indicative of the increasing occurrence of large deals in the market,” the report said.

Multifamily leads as office capital returns

Multifamily was the quarter’s largest asset class at just over $1.7 billion, or 39% of total volume, up 310% year over year. Welltower Inc.’s $414 million purchase of a seniors’ housing portfolio from Amica Senior Lifestyles anchored the quarter.

Office posted the sharpest turnaround, with investment up 278% to $777 million. The largest deal was GWL Realty Advisors’ $243.6 million acquisition of 123 Front St. W. in Toronto from Oxford Properties. GTA-wide office availability fell 190 basis points from a year earlier to 17.6%.

“The improvements in the leasing market have allowed lenders to approach office assets with less apprehension (although this is still submarket- and asset-specific),” the report said.

“With tenant demand rising and little to no new supply in the development pipeline across downtown and suburban markets, investors’ view of the value of existing assets is increasing.”

Damon Conrad, vice-president at REMAX Canada Commercial, flagged the quality divide when investors flooding back to Toronto’s office sector first made headlines this year.

“I think office is seeing clear separation between premium amenity-rich buildings and the older assets that need repositioning,” Conrad told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

Industrial was the laggard. Volume fell 22% to $1.2 billion, and for the first time since Q3 2023, it was not the GTA’s most-traded asset class.

Rate hike tests lender appetite

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on Oct. 28, its first increase since July 2023. Avison Young warned that higher borrowing costs could affect how investors view asset values.

“With signs that both Canada and the US may continue to raise interest rates to combat inflation, there is the possibility that higher borrowing costs could impact investors’ views on asset values and demand for commercial real estate,” the report said.

The average multifamily capitalization rate, the ratio of a property’s net operating income to its sale price, rose 15 basis points to 4.09%.

“Nevertheless, traditional banks and funding sources are still actively seeking lending opportunities, and the situation surrounding tariffs and petroleum supply continues to evolve – with knock-on effects for the Canadian economy and real estate markets,” the report said.

Richard Joy, executive director at the Urban Land Institute in Toronto, has described an uneven recovery, a theme behind equity shortages threatening Canadian commercial refinancing in 2027.

“The GTA’s real estate market is moving at different speeds. Industrial and premium office show signs of recovery, while condominiums remain challenged,” Joy said.

“Investors remain cautious yet generally optimistic heading into the final months of the year,” the report said.

Avison Young expects strong activity in the fourth quarter.

items.title: Bargis: why CIMBC is backing the Canadian Mortgage Awards again
items.description: Coalition’s founder and chief executive officer highlights commitment to brokers, looks ahead to 2027 as CMAs draw closer
items.content: <p>Coalition’s founder and chief executive officer highlights commitment to brokers, looks ahead to 2027 as CMAs draw closer</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639307027915691028.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Coalition’s founder and chief executive officer highlights commitment to brokers, looks ahead to 2027 as CMAs draw closer
items.body:
The Coalition of Independent Mortgage Brokers of Canada (CIMBC) is returning as event partner for next week’s Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs), which mark their 20th year on November 25 at Rebel Toronto.

For John Bargis, the company’s founder and chief executive officer, that support represents an important symbol at a time when mortgage brokers are more important to the homebuying process than ever.

Bargis noted that CIMBC has backed the awards for years and said it was proud to step up again in 2026. “We couldn’t think of a better place to recognize our industry’s accomplishments and awards, and we look forward to a great evening of celebration,” he said.

Excellence Awardees are up for honours in 23 shortlisted categories at Wednesday’s ceremony, with hundreds of industry professionals set to gather from across the country to toast the sector’s best and brightest.

Bargis highlighted the importance of spotlighting the industry’s top performers. “Recognizing excellence matters in any industry because it highlights professionals and innovators who go above and beyond to lead meaningful change,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

“When we celebrate those who truly elevate standards, we raise the bar for all of us that ultimately makes a difference where it counts the most: consumer confidence.”

This year’s ceremony arrives at an important moment for the mortgage market, which has struggled in recent years under the weight of higher interest rates, tariff-driven economic uncertainty, and affordability hurdles in many markets.

Still, that’s not to say the current downturn is unprecedented – and Bargis said he usually takes a long view of market cycles as they play out. “As an industry veteran, I’m often asked whether I’ve ever seen market conditions this challenging,” he said.

“My answer has always been: absolutely, I’ve seen a lot worse. But it doesn’t end there. Markets move in ebbs and flows. Our job is to recognize the opportunities in each cycle and make the adjustments needed to build a sustainable business, rather than chase the same deal as everyone else.”

In that environment, Bargis says he’s advised many CIMBC broker-owners and producing agents on building profitable business plans, including on regulatory and technology changes.

“All they have to do is be willing to step out of their comfort zone and make the necessary changes,” he said. “For those who choose not to, the alternative is far worse – especially in today’s market.”

The outlook for 2027’s mortgage market remains unclear. The Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, with expectations of further rate increases growing as inflation concerns persist.

That rising-rate environment could continue to put the squeeze on borrowers, and Bargis isn’t expecting a big rebound for the housing market. Still, he said there’s opportunity for those who search for it.

“For 2027, unfortunately, all economic indicators point to more of the same,” he said. “That doesn’t mean it’s all bad for those willing to pivot and rethink their business model, something I’ve had to do constantly to stay ahead of the curve.

“We’ve gone from a very robust market to one of more normalcy and stability that will take time to settle. Focus on making the necessary changes and you’ll come through it. Failure to do so will very likely yield unfavourable consequences.”

What CIMBC is prioritizing in the current market

CIMBC is a national coalition of independent, branded brokerages – and Bargis said his priority this year has been making sure the needs of members are met.

“As head of CIMBC, my main focus has been the continued success of our 90-plus independent brokerage brands across the country,” he said.

That work centres on partnerships and education. “We do that by building new strategic lender and industry partnerships and strengthening existing ones, all to improve our brokers’ long-term competitiveness and profitability,” he said. “We also point out growth opportunities, which is critical in slower and more challenging market conditions.”

Why CIMBC stays out of the awards running

The fact that CIMBC doesn’t put itself forward for the Network of the Year award is a deliberate decision by the coalition, Bargis said, consistent over years of backing the event.

“Though often referred to as one, CIMBC is not a network, so it makes no sense for us to be nominated in a category that doesn’t describe our structure or philosophy.”

He pointed to the optics of sponsoring the gala. “As title sponsor of this prestigious gala on a number of occasions, I’m sure you can also appreciate that optically it wouldn’t look right for us to be in the running for an award,” he said. “We’re just happy to be part of it all, and to be showcased throughout the evening by an organization that knows how to put on a great show.”

Bargis highlighted the strong performance of CIMBC’s model over the years, one he believes it would be difficult for others to emulate.

“The greatest compliment to CIMBC’s success, and proof of concept, is that some have recently tried to replicate our model,” he said. “To that, I say: ‘They can imitate, but it’s tough to duplicate.’”

items.description: Rising fixed rates push qualifying income higher across Canada’s biggest housing markets
items.content: <p>Rising fixed rates push qualifying income higher across Canada’s biggest housing markets</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639306974472710524.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rising fixed rates push qualifying income higher across Canada’s biggest housing markets
items.body:
Rising mortgage rates pushed home affordability lower across every major Canadian city in October.

Ratehub.ca’s Home Affordability Report found that buyers in all 13 markets studied needed more qualifying income than the month before, undoing the brief stabilisation affordability had briefly found its footing in September.

The deterioration was driven by rate movements, not prices. The average five-year fixed mortgage rate among Canada’s Big Five banks climbed 43 basis points, from 4.56% in September to 4.99% in October.

Home prices softened in eight of the 13 cities studied, but nowhere by enough to offset the cost of higher borrowing.

Bond yields drive qualifying income higher across Canada

Hamilton, Ontario, saw the sharpest decline.

“Based on our analysis, a borrower would require an additional $7,460 in income to purchase an average-priced home in the city. This was due to a significant rise in mortgage rates (+43 basis points) as well as a $10,300 increase in the local average home price,” Clay Jarvis, mortgage expert at Ratehub.ca in Toronto, explained.

“The Hamilton home buyer in this scenario would pay $217 dollars more on their monthly mortgage payment, or $2,604 per year, if they bought in October rather than September.”

Toronto buyers faced a $6,680 rise in required annual income; Vancouver, $6,650. Halifax, Montréal, and Victoria also recorded increases between $6,050 and $6,680. Edmonton saw the smallest change, at $1,970.

Jarvis identified bond markets as the central pressure point.

“Rates faced constant upward pressure due to elevated bond yields, which were pushed higher by high oil prices and heightened inflation expectations. While most cities saw home prices soften, the declines weren’t enough to offset the impact of higher mortgage rates and stress test qualifying rate.”

What the rate picture means for buyers and brokers

The Bank of Canada’s third-quarter Market Participants Survey results found that 52% of financial market professionals now view rate risks as skewed upward, with the median five-year Government of Canada bond yield forecast rising 35 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.50%.

The best available five-year fixed rate recently dipped 10 basis points to 4.34%, while the best variable rate stood at 3.65% as of November 18, according to Ratehub.ca.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC) in Toronto, warned at the Women in Mortgage Summit Canada in September that fixed rates are likely heading higher still.

“It is a time when we should encourage anyone that is interested in potentially buying a home that they get pre-approved, because today’s rates, even though they’re a little above what they were last week and the week before, they’re only going higher,” Cooper said.

She added: “We have to expect higher interest rates, which also means that fixed-rate mortgages are very attractive now.”

Home sales fell 0.3% from September and were 10.6% lower year-over-year, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).

With the average national sale price just 1.6% below year-ago levels, price declines alone cannot restore the affordability lost to higher rates.
